core: What the Big Bang theory says: the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since
The expansion is the stretching of space itself, not an explosion in space; it began everywhere at once and has no center

The three main lines of evidence, each named with its source: the cosmic microwave background radiation (released at recombination, now about 2.7 K), the redshift of distant galaxies / expansion (Hubble 1929, light stretched by expanding space), and the abundance of light elements (hydrogen and helium from Big Bang nucleosynthesis)

A simple timeline: hot dense early phase, nucleosynthesis in the first minutes, recombination about 380,000 years later when the universe became transparent, then structure formation (first stars and galaxies) over hundreds of millions of years
Common misconceptions corrected factually: the Big Bang was not an explosion in space, and the expansion has no center
What the theory does and does not claim: it explains the universe's evolution from a hot dense state, not what happened before that state or what powered the initial expansion
supporting: Testability of the theory: it predicted the CMB and the helium abundance before they were observed

The CMB discovery story: predicted by Gamow, Alpher, and Herman in the late 1940s; detected by Penzias and Wilson in the mid-1960s (Nobel Prize 1978); COBE (1989), WMAP (2001), and Planck (2009) refined the measurements
Nucleosynthesis detail: about 24-25% of ordinary matter is helium, produced in the first minutes; no elements beyond lithium formed in the Big Bang; heavier elements are made in stars
The dark ages and first stars as the bridge from transparency to galaxies
outOfScope: Large-scale structure of the universe, dark matter, and dark energy (sibling topic universe)
Galaxy types, evolution, and large-scale distribution (sibling topics galaxies, milky-way)
Stellar properties, structure, and life cycles (sibling topics stars, stellar-life-cycle, sun)
Solar system formation and planets (sibling topics solar-system, terrestrial-planets, gas-giants)
Detailed cosmology mathematics (Friedmann equations, inflation models, curvature)

claims.claim: The Big Bang theory holds that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

The expansion of the universe is the stretching of space itself, not galaxies moving through static space; it began everywhere at once, and there is no location where the Big Bang happened, so the expansion has no center.

Edwin Hubble's 1929 observation that galaxies are generally receding from us provided the first major clue for the expanding universe; light from distant galaxies is redshifted because the stretching of space lengthens the light's wavelength as it travels.

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the oldest light we can observe: the leftover glow from the hot early universe, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang when the universe cooled to about 3000 K and became transparent; expansion has stretched that light so that today it is a nearly uniform microwave glow with a temperature of about 2.7 K.

The CMB was predicted in the late 1940s by George Gamow, Ralph Alpher, and Robert Herman and was discovered accidentally in the mid-1960s by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey, who found a faint hiss of radio noise coming from all directions; they received the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery.

Big Bang nucleosynthesis: within the first few minutes (from about one second, when the universe was roughly 10 billion degrees Celsius, to about 3-5 minutes), protons and neutrons fused to form hydrogen, helium, and traces of lithium (NASA also lists beryllium); after that the universe had cooled too much for further element building, so no elements beyond lithium formed in the Big Bang.

The abundance of light elements is evidence for the Big Bang: theory predicts about 24% of the universe's ordinary matter should be helium made in the first minutes, matching observations; stars cannot account for the helium we see (roughly ten times more helium was made in the first four minutes than in all later stars over 10-15 billion years).

Timeline: after recombination at about 380,000 years the universe was transparent but dark (the 'dark ages', roughly 200 million years with no stars); then the first stars, 30 to 300 times more massive than the Sun, formed and over several hundred million years collected into the first galaxies; tiny density fluctuations present in the early universe grew under gravity into the cosmic structures we see today.

The Big Bang theory is testable and has been confirmed by prediction: it predicted both the cosmic microwave background and the helium abundance before they were measured; COBE (launched 1989) measured the CMB as a near-perfect blackbody at 2.73 K, and WMAP (2001) and Planck (2009) refined the measurements, pinning the age at about 13.8 billion years.

The theory does not claim to describe what happened before the hot, dense state, and scientists are not sure what came before inflation or what powered it; the Big Bang theory explains the universe's evolution from that state onward.

The universe is about 13.8 billion years old: NASA's Universe overview states 'around 13.8 billion years ago', WMAP's mission summary gives 13.77 billion years, and OpenStax Astronomy 2e gives a 13.8 billion-year age from the latest observations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The year of the CMB discovery: 1964 or 1965?
positions: OpenStax Astronomy 2e: 'In the mid-1960s, in Holmdel, New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson of AT&T's Bell Laboratories' detected the radiation.
ESA: 'It wasn't until 1964 that it was first detected - accidentally - by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson'.
Commonly cited as 1965, the year Penzias and Wilson published their results.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Penzias and Wilson first noticed the persistent noise in 1964 and published their discovery in 1965. The lesson uses 'in 1965' (the widely used, published date) and keeps the episode framed as an accidental discovery; the evidence packet records both dates.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Age of the universe: 13.77 or 13.8 billion years?
positions: WMAP mission summary: 'the evolution of the universe over 13.77 billion years'.
NASA Universe overview: 'Around 13.8 billion years ago'.
OpenStax Astronomy 2e: 'the 13.8 billion-year age of the universe estimated by the latest observations'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: WMAP's 13.77 and Planck-era 13.8 agree within uncertainty; the lesson states 'about 13.8 billion years' and cites all three.

positions: WMAP mission summary: afterglow light 'emitted about 375,000 years after' the Big Bang.
NASA Universe overview, OpenStax 29.4, and ESA: 'about 380,000 years'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'about 380,000 years', the figure shared by NASA, OpenStax, and ESA; the WMAP figure differs by less than 1.5% and is recorded here.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exactly when in the first minutes did helium form?
positions: NASA Universe overview: 'After five minutes, most of today's helium had formed'.
OpenStax 29.3: helium formed between 3 and 4 minutes at about 900 million K.
WMAP light-elements page: 'During the first three minutes of the universe, most of the deuterium combined to make helium'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All agree helium formed within the first few minutes; the lesson says 'in the first few minutes (roughly 3-5 minutes)' and cites NASA, OpenStax, and WMAP.

positions: WMAP light-elements page: 'about 24% of the ordinary matter in the universe to be helium produced in the Big Bang'.
Textbooks commonly cite about 25% helium by mass.
OpenStax 29.3 stresses the helium excess is unexplained by stars (10x more helium in the first 4 minutes than all stars since).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says 'about a quarter (roughly 24-25%) of the universe's ordinary matter' and cites the WMAP figure.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described 'big bang basics' as a generic foundational concept ('Big Bang Basics is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science', 'a label on a toolbox drawer', 'A college-level explanation names the concept'). These placeholder claims carry no astronomical content and were discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft boilerplate with source-verified content on the Big Bang theory, its three lines of evidence, the early-universe timeline, and common misconceptions.

Checked every figure against NASA, ESA, and OpenStax: 13.8 billion-year age, 380,000-year recombination at about 3000 K, 2.73 K CMB today, 24% helium abundance, 10 billion degrees Celsius at one second, first stars 30-300 solar masses, COBE 1989 / WMAP 2001 / Planck 2009.

Stated explicitly that the Big Bang was not an explosion in space and that the expansion has no center, grounding both statements in OpenStax 29.2 ('space itself stretching... the expansion began everywhere at once... there is no location you can visit where the stretching of space began').
Kept dark matter, dark energy, large-scale structure, galaxies, the Milky Way, and stellar life cycles out of scope, referencing them only as sibling topics.
rightsIssues: NASA and ESA pages are public agency content; OpenStax Astronomy 2e is CC BY 4.0 with an added restriction against ingesting the book into AI/LLM training. All nine sources were used as references for original synthesis only; no diagrams, tables, or source prose were reproduced, so no AI-ingestion issue arises and attribution is handled by the Sources section.

sourceRecords.title: Universe (Overview) - Cosmic History: The Universe's History
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent. Primary source for the timeline: inflation about 13.8 billion years ago; the big bang as the transfer of inflation's energy to matter and light; one second after the big bang at 18 billion degrees Fahrenheit (10 billion degrees Celsius); nucleosynthesis producing hydrogen, helium, and traces of lithium and beryllium, most helium formed by five minutes; recombination about 380,000 years after the big bang when the universe became transparent and released the cosmic microwave background, described as the oldest light we can observe; dark ages of about 200 million years; first stars 30-300 times the Sun's mass; first galaxies over several hundred million years; scientists not sure what came before inflation or what powered it. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: WMAP Overview
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent (this is where the legacy map.gsfc.nasa.gov WMAP education pages now redirect). Supports the universe's age of 13.77 billion years, the timeline of inflation and expansion, the afterglow light seen by WMAP emitted about 375,000 years after the big bang, and WMAP's measurement of the primordial structure that grew into galaxies. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: WMAP's Universe: Big Bang Theory (Big Bang Cosmology)
sourceRecords.notes: The live URL now redirects to the WMAP mission overview; the content was read from an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2023/https://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/bb_theory.html). Supports the Big Bang Model as the broadly accepted theory for the origin and evolution of the universe, postulating that 12-14 billion years ago the portion of the universe we can see today was only a few millimeters across and has since expanded from this hot dense state into the vast, much cooler cosmos, with the cosmic microwave background as the visible remnant; the model rests on general relativity and the cosmological principle. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: WMAP's Universe: Tests of Big Bang Cosmology
sourceRecords.notes: The live URL now redirects to the WMAP mission overview; the content was read from an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2023/https://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/bb_tests.html). Supports the three classic tests of Big Bang cosmology: (1) the expansion of the universe, Edwin Hubble's 1929 observation that galaxies were generally receding; (2) the abundance of the light elements H, He, Li, fused from protons and neutrons in the first few minutes; (3) the cosmic microwave background radiation as remnant heat leftover from the Big Bang. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: WMAP's Universe: Tests of Big Bang - The Light Elements
sourceRecords.notes: The live URL now redirects to the WMAP mission overview; the content was read from an Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/2023/https://map.gsfc.nasa.gov/universe/bb_tests_ele.html). Supports Big Bang nucleosynthesis detail: one second after the Big Bang the temperature was roughly 10 billion degrees, filled with neutrons, protons, electrons, positrons, photons, and neutrinos; during the first three minutes most deuterium combined to make helium with trace lithium; the prediction that about 24% of ordinary matter is helium, in good agreement with observations; Gamow's 1948 hypothesis and Alpher and Herman's work, including the by-product prediction of the CMB with a blackbody spectrum at about 5 K; elements heavier than lithium are synthesized in stars. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: Planck and the Cosmic Microwave Background
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent. Supports: the hot Big Bang state with extremely high density and temperature, the universe expanding ever since (observations since the late 1920s); recombination about 380,000 years after the Big Bang at about 3000 K when electrons combined with protons to form hydrogen atoms and the universe became transparent; CMB photons redshifted by expansion to about 1 mm wavelength and 2.7 K (roughly -270 C); CMB predicted in the late 1940s by Gamow, Alpher, and Herman; detected accidentally by Penzias and Wilson (ESA dates the first detection 1964), Nobel Prize in Physics 1978; COBE (1989) measured a blackbody spectrum at 2.73 K with fluctuations of about 1 part in 100,000 (2006 Nobel to Mather and Smoot); WMAP launched 2001; Planck launched 2009; the CMB's tiny fluctuations grew under gravity into galaxies, clusters, and the large-scale structure. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: 29.2 A Model of the Universe, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (server-rendered HTML). Supports: the expansion as the stretching of space itself rather than galaxies moving through static space; the expansion began everywhere at once; there is no location where the stretching of space began or where the Big Bang happened; redshifts of distant galaxies as light waves stretched by expanding space (a redshift is a stretching of waves); the Hubble constant value 67.3 km/s/Mpc consistent with the 13.8 billion-year age of the universe. Note: OpenStax's page footer restricts using the book to train or ingest into large language models; this lesson uses facts only, with all prose written originally, so no text was ingested. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: 29.3 The Beginning of the Universe, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (server-rendered HTML). Supports: when the universe was about 3 minutes old at about 900 million K, protons and neutrons combined; deuterium and helium formed between 3 and 4 minutes, with a little lithium; no elements beyond lithium could form in the first few minutes; the helium excess in the universe that stars cannot explain; about ten times more helium was manufactured in the first 4 minutes than in all generations of stars during the succeeding 10-15 billion years. Used for original synthesis only.

sourceRecords.title: 29.4 The Cosmic Microwave Background, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (server-rendered HTML). Supports: recombination a few hundred thousand years after the Big Bang (about 380,000 years) when the temperature had dropped to about 3000 K and electrons and nuclei combined into stable hydrogen and helium atoms, ending the scattering of photons and making the universe transparent; the CMB as the afterglow of the hot early universe; Alpher and Herman's prediction of the leftover radiation; Penzias and Wilson's mid-1960s discovery at Bell Laboratories in Holmdel, New Jersey of an unexplained all-sky radio noise (including the pigeons anecdote); their measurement corresponding to 3.5 K; modern measurements of 2.73 K; COBE launched by NASA in November 1989 confirming a 2.73 K blackbody; the 1978 Nobel Prize to Penzias and Wilson. Used for original synthesis only.
